scenarios.q: What does the pool save, and who is keeping track of the connection?

frames.badge: pool empty: open a connection
frames.term:
s = requests.Session()
s.get("https://api.internal/orders")   # pool empty → new connection

lane.note: one TCP connection end to end · the NLB passes it through

frames.b: The pool is empty, so urllib3 opens a connection: TCP handshake, TLS handshake, then the request. An NLB passes TCP straight through, so this is one connection from client to server; the NLB only tracks the flow so it can forward packets.

frames.badge: idle in the pool; three timers start
frames.b: The response arrives and the connection goes back into the pool, idle. Each party starts its own idle timer: the client pool and the Go server have no limit; the NLB will forget the flow at 350 s.

frames.badge: reused: no handshake, timers reset

lane.note: same connection, taken from the pool

frames.b: The next request takes the same connection from the pool. No handshake: the request goes straight out, and every timer drops back to zero.

frames.badge: steady traffic: timers never get close
frames.b: Requests every few seconds keep resetting the timers, so none gets anywhere near its limit. The pool works because every party still believes the connection is open, and steady traffic hides that they each decide that separately.

scenarios.take: A pooled connection is alive only while every party along it agrees it is.
scenarios.gen: Database pools, gRPC channels, Redis clients: anything that keeps a connection open between uses.

scenarios.q: The NLB forgets an idle flow after 350 s; the pool keeps it forever. Traffic pauses for 10 minutes. Why does the next request fail with "connection reset"?

frames.badge: traffic stops; connection idle in the pool
frames.b: The last response comes back and the connection waits in the pool. The client and server timers fill with no limit in sight. The NLB's timer fills toward 350 s.

frames.badge: NLB stops tracking the flow · tells nobody

lane.note: no FIN, no RST: both ends still think it's open

frames.b: At 350 s idle, the NLB stops tracking the flow. It sends nothing to either side. The client and the server both still list the connection as open.

frames.badge: ConnectionResetError: request never reached the server
frames.term:
requests.exceptions.ConnectionError: ('Connection aborted.',
    ConnectionResetError(104, 'Connection reset by peer'))

lane.note: request → NLB has no flow → RST

frames.b: Before reuse, urllib3 checks whether the other side closed the connection. No FIN ever arrived, so it looks fine. The request goes out, the NLB has no flow for it and answers with a TCP RST. Both services are healthy; the request never reached the server.

frames.badge: ALB closes gracefully: client notices, reconnects

lane.note: next request opens a new connection and succeeds

frames.b: An ALB at its 60 s idle limit closes the connection and sends a FIN. urllib3's check before reuse sees it, throws the connection away and opens a fresh one, so usually nothing fails. Only a request sent at the instant the FIN is on its way loses. A silent drop fails every request after a long enough pause.

frames.badge: client gives up first

lane.note: next request opens a new connection and succeeds

frames.h: Fix: the client gives up first
frames.b: Use a pool whose idle expiry is under the load balancer's limit. requests has none; httpx defaults to keepalive_expiry=5.0; Go's default transport uses 90 s, which is under an NLB's 350 s but over an ALB's 60 s. 300 s is drawn here so it shows on the scale.

frames.badge: TCP keepalive keeps the flow alive
frames.term: # SO_KEEPALIVE with an idle time under 350 s (Linux default first probe: 7,200 s)
frames.b: A TCP keepalive probe every few minutes counts as traffic, so the NLB keeps tracking the flow. AWS recommends a keepalive under 350 s for NLB and NAT gateway. As a last line, retry idempotent requests once on a reused connection; urllib3 retries only GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE by default, and requests sets retries to 0 unless you mount an adapter.

scenarios.take: The only party that knew the connection was dead never said so. Make the side that sends requests give up first.
scenarios.gen: AWS NAT gateways (350 s, RST, no FIN) on calls to third-party APIs; database pools that sit idle overnight; stateful firewalls.

scenarios.q: uvicorn closes idle connections after 5 s; the ALB keeps them for 60 s. Why do random 502s appear under light traffic, with nothing in the app's logs?

frames.badge: ALB → target connection idle in the ALB's pool

lane.note: connection X, idle in the ALB's pool

frames.b: An ALB terminates the client's connection and keeps its own pool of connections to each target. On this hop the ALB is the client sending requests and uvicorn is the server. A request just passed on connection X; both timers are filling.

frames.badge: uvicorn closes X: FIN on its way

lane.note: graceful, but it takes a moment to arrive

frames.b: At 5 s idle, uvicorn closes connection X and sends a FIN. That's graceful, but the FIN needs a moment to reach the ALB and be processed.

frames.badge: 502 Bad Gateway · no app log line

lane.note: request sent on X before the FIN was processed

frames.b: A client request arrives in that moment. The ALB picks connection X from its pool, because it hasn't processed the FIN yet, and sends the request. uvicorn's socket is closed, so it answers with an RST. The ALB has nothing to forward and returns 502 Bad Gateway. The app never saw the request, so there is no log line.

frames.badge: light traffic: closes everywhere, an occasional loss
frames.b: Each grey diamond is uvicorn closing a connection after 5 s idle. Under steady load, connections are reused well within 5 s and never reach the limit. Under light or bursty traffic, closes happen all the time, and each is a small window for the race. Most closes are harmless; at that rate, some aren't: a trickle of 502s.

frames.badge: target keep-alive 65 s > ALB 60 s

lane.note: the side that sends requests closes it, so never sends on it again

frames.h: Fix: the side sending requests gives up first
frames.b: Set the target's keep-alive above the ALB's idle timeout. Now the ALB always reaches its limit first and closes the connection itself, and a side never sends a request on a connection it closed. AWS's 502 checklist says exactly this: check "whether the keep-alive duration of the target is shorter than the idle timeout value of the load balancer." Watch HTTPCode_ELB_502_Count; app error rates won't show it.

scenarios.take: Same mistake as scenario 1, on the other hop. Here it surfaces as a 502 at the load balancer, not an exception in the client.
scenarios.gen: nginx or Envoy upstream keep-alive vs the app behind them; Node.js (keepAliveTimeout 5 s) behind any load balancer. gunicorn's sync worker doesn't keep connections alive, so it can't hit this race.

scenarios.q: The pool is exhausted. Why does latency climb while the API's CPU sits idle?

frames.badge: 7.5 of 10 busy · ~50 ms
frames.term:
client = httpx.AsyncClient(limits=httpx.Limits(max_connections=10))
# API answers every call in 50 ms; pool timeout: httpx default 5 s
frames.b: Little's law: connections in use = request rate × time each request holds one. 150 × 0.05 s = 7.5 of 10. A free connection is almost always there. Ten connections at 50 ms can serve at most 10 ÷ 0.05 = 200 requests a second.

frames.badge: needs 15 · pool has 10 · 100 req/s start queueing
frames.b: 300 × 0.05 = 15 connections needed, but the pool allows 10. It still serves 200 req/s; the other 100 req/s wait in the client for a connection to free up.

frames.badge: ≈ 2 s latency · API CPU flat
frames.b: About 400 requests are queued. A new arrival waits 400 ÷ 200 = 2 s for a connection, then 50 ms for the call. Latency climbs about 0.5 s every second. The API still handles only 10 requests at a time, so its CPU is flat; the client's coroutines are just waiting.

frames.badge: PoolTimeout: ≈ 100 of 300 req/s fail
frames.b: Waits reach the 5 s pool timeout and requests start failing with PoolTimeout: about 100 of every 300 per second. The 200 that get through each waited nearly 5 s.

frames.badge: pool of 20 · 15 busy · ~50 ms
frames.h: Fix: size the pool by Little's law
frames.b: Size it for peak rate × p99 latency with headroom (here at least 15, so 20–30), within what the API can actually handle. Keep the pool timeout short so overload fails fast instead of piling up, and measure time waiting for a connection separately from time on the call, or this looks like "the API got slow".

scenarios.take: Nothing is slow and nothing is out of CPU. The bottleneck is a number in a config file, and the latency is all queueing in the client.
scenarios.gen: Database pools, thread pools, worker pools, semaphores: any fixed set of slots with a queue in front. Not every client waits: requests opens and discards extra connections instead.
